title: Representable smooth and etale calculus for arbitrary fibred groupoids
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme], in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention]. Categories fibred in groupoids, morphisms, 2-morphisms and 2-fibre products use [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids]; algebraic spaces use [def-trf-algebraic-space]. For a morphism $f:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of such categories, representable by algebraic spaces means that every scheme 2-base change $\mathcal F\times_{\mathcal G}T$ is equivalent to an algebraic space over $T$. Call a representable map smooth, respectively etale or surjective, when all these algebraic-space projections to $T$ are smooth, respectively etale or surjective. On algebraic spaces smoothness and etaleness are tested on etale scheme charts, using [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-etale-morphism]; surjectivity is surjectivity on field-valued point classes, where two field-valued points are identified if they agree after a common field extension [def-weil-field]. Then representability by algebraic spaces, and each of the properties smooth, etale and surjective for representable maps, are preserved under arbitrary 2-base change and under composition. Every representable etale map is smooth. A morphism $G\to F$ of algebraic spaces, viewed as discrete fibred groupoids, is representable by algebraic spaces. If moreover $G\to F$ is representable in the sense of [def-trf-algebraic-space] (every $h_T\times_FG$ is a scheme), for instance a scheme chart $h_U\to F$, then it is etale, respectively surjective, in the sense of [def-trf-algebraic-space] if and only if it is etale, respectively surjective, as a representable map in the above sense. No stack condition, representable diagonal, or atlas for any of $\mathcal F,\mathcal G$ or the base-changing category is assumed.

This formulation uses the etale-chart convention, so it also applies without an fppf stack hypothesis.

proof.text: Use the triple description of the 2-fibre product. For $f:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$, $a:\mathcal H\to\mathcal G$ and a scheme $T\to\mathcal H$, the equivalence $(\mathcal F\times_{\mathcal G}\mathcal H)\times_{\mathcal H}T\simeq\mathcal F\times_{\mathcal G}T$ sends $(x,h,t,\alpha:f(x)\simeq a(h),\beta:h\simeq t|_{\mathcal H})$ to $(x,t,a(\beta)\alpha)$. Its inverse inserts $h=t|_{\mathcal H}$ and $\beta=1$; the given $\beta$ identifies the other composite with the identity, also on arrows. These formulas commute with restriction. Thus every scheme test of the base-changed map is precisely a scheme test of $f$, up to equivalence over $T$. It is an algebraic space, and its projection has each of the assumed properties of $f$. This proves arbitrary 2-base-change stability, even when $\mathcal H$ is not a stack.

For composable representable maps $f:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ and $g:\mathcal G\to\mathcal K$, fix $T\to\mathcal K$. Put $B=\mathcal G\times_{\mathcal K}T$, an algebraic space by representability of $g$. Apply the representable-pullback-over-space lemma to $f$ and $B\to\mathcal G$: $A=\mathcal F\times_{\mathcal G}B$ is an algebraic space. Identify $A\simeq\mathcal F\times_{\mathcal K}T$ as follows. A triple $(x,(y,t,\gamma:g(y)\simeq t),\alpha:f(x)\simeq y)$ goes to $(x,t,\gamma g(\alpha))$. The inverse inserts $y=f(x)$ and $\alpha=1$; $\alpha$ identifies its composite with the identity. The same formulas on arrows and restrictions give an equivalence over $T$. Therefore $gf$ is representable. No diagonal or atlas of any of the three groupoids was used.

Retain $A\to B\to T$ from step 2, and let $P$ be smooth or etale, assumed for both $f$ and $g$. The scheme-locality lemma verifies the hypotheses of the presentation criterion for this $P$. Choose an etale surjective scheme atlas $V\to B$. Then $E=A\times_BV\simeq\mathcal F\times_{\mathcal G}V\to V$ has $P$ by the scheme test of $f$. Choose an etale surjective scheme atlas $U\to E$. The presentation criterion applied over the scheme $V$ says that $U\to V$ has $P$. Likewise the test $B\to T$ of $g$, with source chart $V$ and target chart $T$, gives $P(V\to T)$. Scheme composition gives $P(U\to T)$. The map $E\to A$ is the base change of the etale surjective atlas $V\to B$, so it is etale surjective; its composite with $U\to E$ is an etale surjective scheme chart $U\to A$. The presentation criterion for $A\to T$, with this chart and target chart $T$, now gives $P(A\to T)$. This proves both composition assertions on every scheme test.

proof.text: For surjectivity of the composite, keep the same test $T$, $B$ and $A$. Given a field-valued point $t:\operatorname{Spec}K\to T$, surjectivity of $B\to T$ gives an extension $K\hookrightarrow L$ and a lift $b\in B(L)$ of $t|_L$. Apply the surjectivity test of $f$ to the scheme map $\operatorname{Spec}L\to B\to\mathcal G$. It gives an extension $L\hookrightarrow M$ and an object $x$ with $f(x)\simeq b|_M$ in $\mathcal G(M)$. Together with the $T$-component of $b|_M$, these are an $M$-valued point of $A$ mapping to $t|_M$. Equality in the representing algebraic space is the isomorphism class of this triple. This proves surjectivity on point classes. Only two successive field extensions and the definition of a 2-fibre product are involved; in particular no descent of objects in the original groupoids is asserted.

For an etale representable $f$, fix its algebraic-space test $X\to T$. Choose a presentation of this map with etale surjective source chart $U\to X$ and etale target chart $V\to T$. The etale version of the presentation criterion makes $U\to V$ an etale scheme map. The scheme etale-implies-smooth lemma makes it smooth. The smooth version of the same criterion makes $X\to T$ smooth. Scheme etale locality and smooth locality are the hypotheses needed for the two applications of that criterion. Since $T$ was arbitrary, $f$ is smooth.

For a morphism $G\to F$ of algebraic spaces, a scheme test is the sheaf fibre product $G\times_Fh_T$, an algebraic space by the algebraic-space fibre-product lemma. The groupoids involved are discrete, so its ordinary pairs of sections are exactly the triples of the 2-fibre product: the isomorphism component exists precisely for equal images and is then unique. Hence every such morphism is representable by algebraic spaces. If it is additionally representable by schemes, each test projection $W\to T$ is a scheme morphism. The presentation criterion and scheme-locality lemma say that its chartwise etaleness is equivalent to its scheme etaleness. Thus the two meanings of etale for this representable map agree test by test.

For the remaining comparison, consider any scheme test projection $W\to T$ of a scheme-representable map. If it is topologically surjective, for $t:\operatorname{Spec}K\to T$ its pullback $W_K\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ is surjective by scheme surjectivity under base change. Choose a point $w\in W_K$; its residue field $L=\kappa(w)$ gives a $K$-extension and a lift in $W(L)$. Conversely apply field-extension lifting to the canonical point $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t)\to T$ of any $t\in|T|$: a lift over an extension has an image point of $W$ above $t$, proving topological surjectivity. These arguments also cover empty schemes. Therefore the scheme-test definitions of surjectivity agree. A chart $h_U\to F$ is representable by schemes by definition, so both comparison conclusions apply to it. Every argument above used atlases only for the algebraic spaces produced by tests, never for the original fibred groupoids.
